title: Fused-Planes: Why Train a Thousand Tri-Planes When You Can Share?
claim: Under a fixed training budget, our compact representation renders sharper detail with far less memory than baseline representations.
layout: 4 columns left-to-right, each with zoom-in insets and size/PSNR captions
description: A single row of four renderings of the same white car, one per method: K-Planes, Tri-Planes, Fused-Planes-ULW and Fused-Planes. Each rendering has two zoom-in insets at its right. A blue box marks the roof and window area, and a pink box marks the front wheel. Matching colored frames on the insets let the reader compare detail across methods. Below each image are the method name, the model size in MB and the PSNR. The best values are bold and the second-best are underlined. The K-Planes and Tri-Planes cars look blurry and noisy with ragged edges. The two Fused-Planes cars look cleaner and show clearer wheels. Sizes range from 410.1 MB down to 0.0008 MB, so the eye goes first to the colored insets and then to the numbers.
caption: Comparison of planar representations under the same budget. Our method achieves the best rendering quality and the best memory footprint among planar representations when training large classes of 3D objects under a fixed time budget (7 minutes per object in this illustration). Fused-Planes-ULW designates the ultra-lightweight variant of Fused-Planes.
abstract: Tri-Planar NeRFs enable the application of powerful 2D vision models for 3D tasks, by representing 3D objects using 2D planar structures. This has made them the prevailing choice to model large collections of 3D objects. However, training Tri-Planes to model such large collections is computationally intensive and remains largely inefficient. This is because the current approaches independently train one Tri-Plane per object, hence overlooking structural similarities in large classes of objects. In response to this issue, we introduce Fused-Planes, a novel object representation that improves the resource efficiency of Tri-Planes when reconstructing object classes, all while retaining the same planar structure. Our approach explicitly captures structural similarities across objects through a latent space and a set of globally shared base planes. Each individual Fused-Planes is then represented as a decomposition over these base planes, augmented with object-specific features. Fused-Planes showcase state-of-the-art efficiency among planar representations, demonstrating $7.2 \times$ faster training and $3.2 \times$ lower memory footprint than Tri-Planes while maintaining rendering quality. An ultra-lightweight variant further cuts per-object memory usage by $1875 \times$ with minimal quality loss. Our project page can be found at https://fused-planes.github.io .
